problem: Social navigation research either hand-tunes geometric planners, which cannot handle all social situations (unsafe or the frozen robot problem), or discards them for end-to-end learned planners that lose safety, explainability and testability and suffer distribution shift.
motivation: Practitioners still deploy geometric stacks in the real world. A case study on SCAND shows geometric planners already match human demonstrations in most scenarios (up to 80%), and fail only in a small share (about 5%) that needs social reasoning. This suggests combining the two paradigms rather than replacing geometric planners.
key_idea: Use a geometric planner (move_base) as the backbone and a learned gating classifier that switches to a behavior-cloning policy only in scenarios where the geometric plan is predicted to be socially non-compliant.
insight: On SCAND playback, BC beats move_base in-distribution but degrades out-of-distribution, while move_base stays unchanged. The hybrid tracks the better of the two on both test sets (Fig. 4). In the human study the hybrid is most consistent across scenarios and robots, and hysteresis voting plus a geometric fallback near obstacles are needed to make it stable on real robots.
method: Social compliance definition: a plan is compliant if the undirected Hausdorff distance to the human demonstration waypoints (up to a 10 m goal, from 2 s of sensor history) is below a threshold ε (ε=1.0 used in the case study).
Geometric benchmarking: move_base (Dijkstra+DWA), move_base with social layer, Human-Aware Planner and CoHAN are replayed on SCAND with default parameters and compared by CDFs of Hausdorff distance.
Learned planner Lθ: behavior cloning trained only on scenarios where the geometric plan is non-compliant (D_N, d>ε), regressing the demonstration trajectory.
Gating classifier Mϕ: a cross-entropy classifier predicting from the scenario whether the geometric plan C(S_t) is compliant (c_t=1 if d≤ε), choosing C or Lθ at each step.

Deployment engineering: a hysteresis vote over the past n steps with threshold r for switching, and a forced switch to the geometric planner for t seconds when within p meters of an obstacle; the values are set empirically per site and robot.

Evaluation: SCAND playback plus an extra out-of-distribution set collected in the lab (intersection, frontal approach, following), and a human study with Jackal (GMU) and Spot (UT) in Frontal Approach, Intersection and Narrow Doorway.

setting.backbone: move_base (DWA + Dijkstra) geometric planner + behavior cloning policy + learned binary gating classifier (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: SCAND (8.7 h, 138 trajectories, 25 miles of teleoperated social navigation demonstrations); extra lab-collected demonstrations used only as an OOD test set
setting.observation: RGB images, 3D LiDAR / BEV costmap, odometry (past 2 s of sensor observations)
setting.action_space: planned waypoint trajectories executed as velocity commands via the geometric local planner or BC
setting.simulator: none; SCAND dataset playback and real world

numbers.extra: Results only shown as CDF curves of Hausdorff distance (Fig. 4); no numeric values

numbers_note: No standard embodied navigation benchmark. The SCAND playback results are only given as CDF figures. The human-study numbers are Likert averages from Table I.
results: Geometric planners align with human demonstrations (Hausdorff < 1.0 m) in up to 80% of SCAND scenarios, with move_base best. The hybrid matches the better of move_base and BC on both in-distribution and OOD playback. In the human study it has the highest or near-highest scores in most cases, e.g. Jackal Frontal 4.04 vs 2.66 (move_base) and 3.63 (BC). On Doorway, move_base is slightly higher for Jackal (4.08 vs 3.89), and BC is higher for Spot on Q-averages in Frontal/Doorway only marginally.
limitations: Proof of concept: BC is a simple baseline, and the gating and hysteresis parameters are tuned empirically per site and robot.
Compliance is defined as closeness to a single human demonstration, but other socially compliant behaviors may exist.
Small human study (10 participants per scenario) with only three scenarios; the hybrid is not always best (e.g. Jackal Doorway).
